title: Better Learning-Augmented Spanning Tree Algorithms via Metric Forest Completion
claim: A cheap, imperfect forest prediction can be completed with a few extra edges into a spanning tree close to the optimal one.
layout: 4 panels in a row, left-to-right, colored convex hulls around clusters
description: Four side-by-side panels show the same set of 100 points drawn as black dots linked by thin black edges. Each tree component is wrapped in a translucent colored convex hull (cyan, orange, pink, green, blue, red, teal, olive). Panel (a), 'Kruskal stopped early', shows disconnected clusters with no links between them. Panel (b), 'Completed MST', adds the long connecting edges that join the clusters into the full minimum spanning tree. Panel (c), 'Initial forest (P; {T_i})', shows a slightly different clustering, which acts as the heuristic prediction. Panel (d), 'MFC solution', adds connecting edges between the predicted clusters to form a complete spanning tree. The eye goes first to the large cyan hull and the bright colors. Captions below each panel are short labels.
caption: (a) The forest obtained by terminating Kruskal's algorithm early for a set of 100 points. (b) Running Kruskal's algorithm to the end leads to a full MST. (c) The initial forest can be viewed as a heuristic prediction for the forest in (a). For this example, $\gamma(\mathcal{P}) \approx 1.06$. (d) Solving metric forest completion problem produces a full spanning tree that approximates the true MST.
abstract: We present improved learning-augmented algorithms for finding an approximate minimum spanning tree (MST) for points in an arbitrary metric space. Our work follows a recent framework called metric forest completion (MFC), where the learned input is a forest that must be given additional edges to form a full spanning tree. Veldt et al. (2025) showed that optimally completing the forest takes $Î©(n^2)$ time, but designed a 2.62-approximation for MFC with subquadratic complexity. The same method is a $(2Î³+ 1)$-approximation for the original MST problem, where $Î³\geq 1$ is a quality parameter for the initial forest. We introduce a generalized method that interpolates between this prior algorithm and an optimal $Î©(n^2)$-time MFC algorithm. Our approach considers only edges incident to a growing number of strategically chosen ``representative'' points. One corollary of our analysis is to improve the approximation factor of the previous algorithm from 2.62 for MFC and $(2Î³+1)$ for metric MST to 2 and $2Î³$ respectively. We prove this is tight for worst-case instances, but we still obtain better instance-specific approximations using our generalized method. We complement our theoretical results with a thorough experimental evaluation.
